facts.text: On this date in 1938, Orson Welles' War of the Worlds broadcast caused widespread panic — but the hysteria was largely invented by newspapers eager to discredit radio as a rival news medium.
On October 30, 1961, the Soviet Union detonated Tsar Bomba, the largest nuclear device ever tested. Its shockwave circled the Earth three times.
Manila is the most densely populated city on Earth, packing over 111,000 people per square kilometer — denser than any other city by a significant margin.
Canada has more lakes than every other country on Earth combined, holding roughly 60% of the world's fresh surface lake water within its borders.
Niger has the world's highest total fertility rate, averaging around 6.7 children per woman — meaning its population is projected to nearly quadruple by 2100.
On Oct 30, 1929 — the day after Black Tuesday — the Dow rebounded 12.3%. Markets were so volatile that a single day's recovery briefly convinced many the crash was over. It was not.

On Oct 30, 1974, Muhammad Ali beat Foreman in Zaire. Promoter Don King, nearly broke beforehand, parlayed the payout into a boxing empire worth hundreds of millions — one of sport's greatest capital launches.

The entire US Treasury bond market, the largest securities market on earth, has no central exchange. Trillions change hands daily through a loose network of dealers making phone calls and sending messages.

Warren Buffett's Berkshire Hathaway originally made textiles. He later called buying it the worst investment of his life — the brand name notwithstanding, the mills were a cash trap he spent years unwinding.

The Amsterdam Stock Exchange, founded in 1602, introduced short selling, options, and margin trading within its first decade. Regulators tried to ban short selling almost immediately. It didn't work then either.
On this date in 1961, the Soviet Union detonated Tsar Bomba — still the largest explosion in human history. Its shockwave circled Earth three times.
Your skeleton is not static. Every 10 years, your body has replaced virtually every bone cell you had, rebuilding you from the inside out.
On this date in 1938, Orson Welles broadcast War of the Worlds. The panic it caused was itself a myth — newspapers, threatened by radio, invented the mass hysteria story.
A neutron star packs more mass than the Sun into a sphere the size of a city. A teaspoon of its matter would weigh roughly a billion tons on Earth.
Trees in a forest share carbon and chemical signals through fungal networks in the soil, with larger trees actively subsidizing smaller, shaded seedlings nearby.
On this day in 1938, Orson Welles' War of the Worlds broadcast panicked America — the same year the first Superman comic was printed. Both men were 22.
Oxford University was already 300 years old when the Aztec Empire was founded. Medieval England predates Montezuma.
On this day in 1945, the last German U-boat surrendered — six months after Hitler died, the war's final holdouts were still fighting a war their leader had already lost.
Cleopatra lived closer in time to the Moon landing than to the construction of the Great Pyramid. Ancient Egypt spans more history than we've had since.
Nintendo was founded in 1889, making it older than the Eiffel Tower, older than the zipper, and older than the very concept of a world war.
Sonder (n.): the realization that each passerby has a life as vivid and complex as your own. Coined by John Koenig in The Dictionary of Obscure Sorrows, 2012. Already it feels ancient.
Hiraeth (n.): a Welsh longing for a home you cannot return to — or never had. Untranslatable, it folds grief, nostalgia, and belonging into a single breath.
On this date in 1938, Orson Welles broadcast War of the Worlds. The word 'panic' comes from Pan, the Greek god whose sudden appearances were said to cause irrational, overwhelming dread.
Petrichor (n.): the smell of rain on dry earth. Named in 1964 by Australian scientists Bear and Thomas, from Greek petra (stone) and ichor, the fluid that flowed through the veins of the gods.

On October 30, 1925, John Logie Baird made the first true television transmission. The word 'television' blends Greek tele (far) and Latin visio (sight) — a hybrid that purists at the time found grotesque.
On Oct 30, 2013, the world's first Bitcoin ATM went live at a Vancouver coffee shop. It processed $10,000 in transactions within its first week, charging a 3% fee.
On Oct 30, 2008, Satoshi Nakamoto's Bitcoin whitepaper was quietly posted to a cryptography mailing list. It had nine pages and zero replies for two days.
Ethereum's 'difficulty bomb' was deliberately coded into the protocol to make proof-of-work mining progressively unviable — a timed forcing function to compel the switch to proof-of-stake.
The DAO hack of 2016 didn't exploit a bug in Ethereum itself. It exploited a reentrancy flaw in The DAO's own Solidity code, draining 3.6M ETH before anyone could respond.
Bitcoin's UTXO model means your wallet balance doesn't technically exist. What exists is a set of unspent outputs scattered across thousands of blocks, assembled on the fly when you spend.

On this date in 1956, the Dartmouth AI conference proposal was formally circulated for funding — the document that coined 'artificial intelligence' as a field name, written by McCarthy, Minsky, Shannon, and Rochester.

On this date in 2019, OpenAI released the full GPT-2 model after a staged rollout it had delayed citing misuse risk — the first time a lab treated a language model release as a biosecurity-style decision.

AlphaFold 2 predicted protein structures for nearly every known protein in UniProt — roughly 200 million structures — in weeks. Experimental X-ray crystallography would have taken the field thousands of years.

Training GPT-4 is estimated to have required around 10^25 floating-point operations. The human brain performs roughly 10^15 synaptic operations per second — meaning training consumed more compute than a brain does in 300 years.
The transformer architecture, now foundational to virtually every frontier AI system, was introduced in a 2017 paper by eight Google researchers. Six of the eight authors have since left Google.
